rv.q: I do know that my sadness at their loss was mixed with joy that McNally had indirectly captured something of their voices in his characterization of the ultimate Voice—Callas.
Tyne Daly is doing something extraordinary in Master Class
Even so, “Master Class” remains a diverting and at times juicily amusing vehicle for an actress capable of bottling a prima donna’s blunt-force charisma.
This paradox is the magic trick at the center of Tyne Daly’s remarkable performance as Maria Callas in “Master Class,” Terrence McNally’s 1995 play about the twilight of that goddess of bel canto.
Daly is sometimes ragged, but always courageous.
Daly brings something better to the character — a sense of vulnerable humanity that makes her courage to survive all the more admirable.
All praise to the company for bringing it back to the East Coast stage again.
This Master Class contains a kind of Pyrrhic victory, an intrepidly honest performance that reveals a smart, yet tangibly scant show.
And the gamble doesn’t quite pay off.
Stripping La Divina of both mastery and class, McNally shrinks her with a vengeance.
Well, that is who she was, as we learn from a playwright who knows whereof he speaks and from Daly’s triumphant portrayal of her.
She shines as she plays Callas with the solid authority one would expect of the opera singer people cheered as La Divina, and with a real handle on Callas' regrets, quirks and demons.
Even if the play is essentially a monologue mixed with some opera selections, it makes for a thrilling ride and is one of McNally's most compelling works.
The portrait is complicated and charismatic.
Her ego rises above her generosity of spirit making her Callas an unforgettable monster.
McNally's well-crafted, quip-filled drama — which depicts Callas teaching at Juilliard, circa 1971 — is less a biography and more a love letter to La Divina.
These patches don’t come off because the writing is so soap-operatic.
But by Act Two, when Maria is more focused on actually transforming her students at any cost, Tyne is earthy, sharp, bitchy, and moving.
Daly, a forceful, convincingly complex presence in the coaching scenes, seems uncertain and unfocussed in the reveries (where Stephen Wadsworth's scattershot staging doesn't help).
This Master Class may entertaining in some ways, but it�s never true � and it doesn�t take long for false to stop being fun.
Daly delivers a commanding performance that is a master class all by itself.
But Zoe Caldwell, who played Callas in the original Broadway production, was wrong, and Tyne Daly, for all her talent and appealing modesty, seems largely correct.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this McNally revival, with most praising Tyne Daly's courageous, deeply human portrayal of Callas, even if a few find her miscast. The production earns mostly warm notices despite some reservations about the play itself.

vs.sum: The Samuel J. Friedman Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and a well-raked mezzanine, ensuring a clear view from most seats. The sound quality is consistently praised, and the seating is comfortable with decent legroom. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant design following renovation, though facilities like restrooms are average, leading to some congestion during intermissions.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. Built-in induction loop for t-coil hearing aids.
